passage:
January 1st: Kalyani wrote in big letters on the first page of her diary: THIS YEAR I WILL BE GOOD AT MATHS. She drew three stars around it.
February: Her maths marks were the same as before, 11 out of 25. She looked at the stars and felt silly. "I tried," she told Ritu didi. "What did you actually do?" Ritu asked. Kalyani couldn't think of anything.
March: Ritu helped her write something new on a sticky note: "Five sums after tea. Tick the box." Kalyani stuck it on the fridge. Every day after tea she did five sums, then ticked a box. By the end of March there were twenty-six ticks, and her unit test said 17 out of 25.

qa.q: What did the sticky note on the fridge say?
qa.a: "Five sums after tea. Tick the box."

qa.q: Why did Kalyani feel silly looking at the stars in February?
qa.a: She had made a big promise but her marks hadn't changed, and she realised she hadn't actually done anything specific.

qa.q: Why did 'five sums after tea' work when the big promise didn't?
qa.a: It was small, clear and at a set time, so it was easy to start each day and easy to check with a tick.

qa.q: How might Ritu didi feel seeing twenty-six ticks on the fridge?
qa.a: Ritu didi may feel proud that her question, 'What did you actually do?', helped Kalyani find a plan that worked 😊.

grounding: Over three months, a girl's vague vow to be good at maths does nothing until she sets five sums after tea.

passage: Jahnavi, every new year you say you'll "get better at maths", na? Your Akash dadu used to say exactly that. When I was nine, in Cuttack, I promised my mother every Sunday: "This week I'll study hard." And every Sunday I had done nothing, because what does "study hard" even mean at nine? My marks stayed at the bottom. Then our maths teacher, Pattnaik sir, gave me a different kind of promise. "Akash, after your evening milk, do five sums from page thirty. Only five. Show me on Monday." Five! I could do five. I did them every evening, then five more from page thirty-one. By the end of term I was in the middle of the class. Not the top, mind you. But the middle felt like a mountain.

qa.q: What did Pattnaik sir tell Akash to do after his evening milk?
qa.a: Do five sums from page thirty, only five, and show them on Monday.

qa.q: Why did young Akash do nothing after promising to 'study hard'?
qa.a: The promise was vague, so young Akash felt lost about where to begin, and each week slipped by with no clear step to take.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try this year instead of promising to 'get better at maths'?
qa.a: Jahnavi could set a small, specific goal, like five sums at a fixed time each day, which is easy to start and to check.

qa.q: How might Akash's mother have felt about the Sunday promises?
qa.a: She may have felt hopeful each Sunday and disappointed each week, without knowing the promise itself had no clear step in it.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how vague promises to study hard did nothing until a teacher set five sums after his evening milk.

passage: Swati's family lived in one room in a crowded Mumbai lane, and in the evenings it was loud: the TV next door, her little brother Yogesh singing, the pressure cooker whistling. For weeks she had been telling herself, "I have to get better at maths," but every evening the noise won, and she did nothing. With the half-yearly exam three weeks away, she tried something new. She wrote on the wall calendar: "After tea: 5 problems." Only five. She took her notebook to the steps outside, where it was quieter, and finished five before the streetlight came on. Yogesh came to count them with her. On the calendar she drew a small tick each day. After two weeks, the fractions that used to scare her looked almost ordinary.

qa.q: What did Swati write on the wall calendar?
qa.a: "After tea: 5 problems."

qa.q: Why did 'I have to get better at maths' lead to nothing for weeks?
qa.a: It was a big, vague wish with no starting point, so on each noisy evening Swati felt stuck and it was easy to put off.

qa.q: Which choices helped Swati follow through despite the noise?
qa.a: She set a small, specific target at a fixed time, moved to the quieter steps and ticked each day, which made starting easy and progress visible.

qa.q: What might counting the problems with Swati mean for Yogesh?
qa.a: Yogesh gets to be part of his sister's effort, which may make him proud and gives Swati a small, cheerful audience.

grounding: In a noisy one-room home with an exam near, a girl turns a vague vow into five problems after tea.

passage:
In their flat in Shillong, Damini wrote on the first page of her rough notebook: I WILL BE BETTER AT MATHS. She underlined it three times.
For two weeks nothing happened. Every evening she thought about being better at maths, then played carrom with Lalremsiami from the next flat.
After the test (9 out of 25), Lalremsiami said, 'Better how? Like, what do you actually do?'
Damini didn't know.
So they made a rule and wrote it on a sticky note on the fridge: 5 SUMS AFTER TEA. Then carrom.
The first evening, five sums took twenty minutes. By Friday they took twelve. Every day Damini put a tick on the note. When the next test came, she got 17, and there were fourteen ticks on the fridge.

qa.q: What was written on the sticky note on the fridge?
qa.a: 5 SUMS AFTER TEA.

qa.q: Why did nothing happen for two weeks after Damini wrote 'I will be better at maths'?
qa.a: Writing the wish made Damini feel hopeful, but it gave her nothing to actually do each evening, so she thought about it and then played carrom.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did the new goal work?
qa.a: Lalremsiami's question, 'What do you actually do?'; five sums after tea was small, easy to start and easy to tick, so Damini could see progress.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel seeing fourteen ticks on the fridge?
qa.a: Lalremsiami would likely feel proud of helping, since one simple question turned Damini's big wish into something she could do every day. 🙂

grounding: A child's vague vow to do better at maths goes nowhere until it becomes five sums after tea, a small goal she can start and check.

passage:
'This time I'm really going to get better at Hindi,' Aditi announced at dinner.
'You said that last term,' Ishita didi said, tearing her roti.
'This time I mean it.'
'Okay. What will you do tomorrow?'
Aditi blinked. 'Get better.'
'That's not something you do. That's a wish.' Ishita pointed at the Hindi book on the shelf. 'How about this: read one page aloud to me every night after dinner, and write down two new words.'
'Only one page?'
'One page. Every night. I'll tick it.'
The next evening Aditi appeared with the book before Ishita had finished eating. 'One page. Listen.' She stumbled on 'prashansa' and wrote it down.
'That's one,' Ishita said, and drew the first tick on the calendar.

qa.q: Which word did Aditi stumble on and write down?
qa.a: 'Prashansa'.

qa.q: Why did Aditi blink when asked what she would do tomorrow?
qa.a: Aditi was surprised and a little confused, realising she had no actual plan; 'get better' felt like a goal but gave her nothing concrete to start with.

qa.q: What turned Aditi's wish into something she could act on?
qa.a: Ishita's specific target, one page read aloud and two new words every night, ticked on the calendar; small and checkable, so Aditi started the very next evening.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Aditi turns up with the book before dinner is finished?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels pleased and a bit amused that the plan is working, and glad to be part of her sister's progress.

grounding: A child's vague promise to get better at Hindi becomes a specific nightly target that is easy to start and check.
